concepts.name: Vijayanagara Architectural Style: Defining Features and Regional Synthesis
key_dimensions: Distinguishing features: tall ornate gopurams, pillared mandapas, enclosure walls, and horse motifs on pillars
Synthesis of Chalukya, Hoysala, Chola, and Pandya architectural traditions
Contrast with contemporaneous Bahmani/Deccan Sultanate architecture to identify UPSC trap questions on 'unique' features
Use of hard granite as primary material vs. softer sandstone in northern traditions

concepts.name: Gopuram: Evolution and Significance in Vijayanagara Temples
key_dimensions: Shift in emphasis from the main vimana (tower over sanctum) to the gopuram under Vijayanagara patronage — a key UPSC trap
Progressive increase in height and decorative elaboration as a dynastic statement of power
Comparison with earlier Dravidian gopurams (Pallava, Chola) to highlight Vijayanagara's distinct contribution
Iconic examples: gopurams at Hampi's Virupaksha temple and Srirangam (Vijayanagara additions)

concepts.name: Virupaksha Temple, Hampi: Architectural and Religious Significance
key_dimensions: Status as the royal temple and its continuity from pre-Vijayanagara period — trap: it was not built by Vijayanagara rulers but expanded by them
Key structural additions: large gopuram, mandapas, and pillared halls added by successive rulers
Dedicatory deity (Shiva as Virupaksha/Pampapati) and its link to dynastic legitimacy
UNESCO World Heritage Site context and its position within the 'Sacred Centre' of Hampi

concepts.name: Vitthala Temple Complex, Hampi: Pinnacle of Vijayanagara Architecture
key_dimensions: Identification as the most spectacular example of Vijayanagara architectural achievement
The iconic Stone Chariot (actually a shrine for Garuda) — frequently confused as a 'chariot' in questions
Musical pillars (sapta-svara pillars) — their acoustic properties and examinable uniqueness
Patron association: primarily built/expanded under Krishnadevaraya, with earlier foundations

concepts.name: Krishnadevaraya's Architectural Patronage: Style and Innovations
key_dimensions: Introduction of the 'Rayagopura' style — taller, more elaborate gateways as imperial statements
Construction of Hazara Rama temple and Krishna temple at Hampi as specific examples
Patronage of temples outside Hampi: Tirupati, Chidambaram, Srirangam expansions
Comparison with his literary patronage (Amuktamalyada) to assess integrated cultural policy questions

concepts.name: Hazara Rama Temple: Narrative Sculpture and Royal Ritual Space
key_dimensions: Function as the private royal chapel rather than a public temple — a key distinguishing feature
Exterior walls covered with continuous narrative friezes depicting scenes from the Ramayana
Inner mandapa pillars with scenes from Krishnalila and royal processions — source for social history
Use as primary evidence for reconstructing Vijayanagara court ceremonies and festivals like Mahanavami

concepts.name: Mahanavami Dibba (Royal Platform): Function and Architectural Form
key_dimensions: Identification as a stepped platform used for the Navaratri/Mahanavami festival — not a temple structure
Carved relief panels depicting royal processions, animal fights, dancing girls, and foreign visitors
Value as a primary source for understanding Vijayanagara court culture and military organization
Distinction from other platforms in the 'Royal Centre' of Hampi to avoid UPSC confusion questions

concepts.name: Thousand-Pillared Mandapa: Concept, Examples, and Symbolic Purpose
key_dimensions: Distinction between the concept of 'thousand-pillared' (symbolic, rarely exactly 1000) and literal count — a common UPSC trap
Examples: Vitthala temple's main mandapa, and temples at Lepakshi and Srisailam
Architectural function: assembly hall (kalyana mandapa), public worship space vs. inner sanctum
Sculptural program on pillars — rearing horses with riders as a distinctly Vijayanagara motif

concepts.name: Lepakshi Temple Complex (Veerabhadra Temple): Art and Architecture
key_dimensions: Built during the reign of Achyutaraya by brothers Virupanna and Viranna — local governors, not the king directly
Famous for the unfinished hanging pillar (one of 70 pillars that does not rest on the ground) — frequently cited in questions
Exceptional mural paintings: considered the finest surviving example of Vijayanagara fresco painting
Large monolithic Nandi and the open-air Nagalinga as iconic sculptural achievements

concepts.name: Vijayanagara Mural Painting Tradition: Technique, Themes, and Survival
key_dimensions: Technique: fresco-secco method (painting on dry plaster) vs. true fresco — an important art history distinction
Primary surviving examples: Lepakshi (Veerabhadra temple) and Virupaksha temple (Hampi)
Themes: scenes from Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata Purana, and royal court life
Stylistic features: bold outlines, flat colors, elongated figures — contrast with Ajanta or Mughal miniature styles

concepts.name: Vijayanagara Sculpture: Iconographic Conventions and Stylistic Identity
key_dimensions: Characteristic features: elongated torsos, elaborate jewelry, rigid posture — distinction from fluid Hoysala or sensuous Chola sculpture
Preference for large monolithic sculptures: Sasivekalu Ganesha, Kadalekalu Ganesha, and Ugra Narasimha at Hampi
Ugra Narasimha (Lakshminarasimha) monolith — often confused; originally had Lakshmi on his lap, now damaged
Integration of sculpture into architectural programs (pillar sculpture) vs. freestanding icons

concepts.name: Secular and Civil Architecture at Hampi: Royal Centre Structures
key_dimensions: Key structures: Lotus Mahal (zenana enclosure), Elephant Stables, Queen's Bath — demonstrating Islamic architectural influence
The Lotus Mahal: Indo-Islamic synthesis with cusped arches and lotus-bud finials, located in the 'Zenana Enclosure'
Elephant Stables: eleven chambers with alternating domed roofs showing Persian/Deccan Sultanate influence
Significance as evidence of cosmopolitan cultural exchange and Vijayanagara's pragmatic adoption of foreign styles

concepts.name: Indo-Islamic Synthesis in Vijayanagara Architecture: Scope and Limits
key_dimensions: Elements borrowed: cusped arches, stucco ornamentation, dome forms — primarily in secular/civil structures
Strict retention of Dravidian/Agamic traditions in religious temple architecture — the critical boundary UPSC exploits
Reasons for synthesis: presence of Muslim soldiers, traders, and craftsmen in Vijayanagara service
Comparison with Mughal syncretism to highlight the difference in context and degree of integration

concepts.name: Hampi (Vijayanagara) as a UNESCO World Heritage Site: Components and Zones
key_dimensions: Inscribed in 1986 under criteria (i), (iii), (iv) — cultural landscape of Outstanding Universal Value
Division into 'Sacred Centre' (temples, ghats) and 'Royal Centre' (palaces, platforms) — a spatial distinction tested in Prelims
Ongoing threat: the site is on the UNESCO 'List of World Heritage in Danger' — year of listing (1999) and reasons (illegal construction, encroachment)
Distinction from the nearby 'Tungabhadra' river setting and its role in the sacred geography of the site

concepts.name: Dynastic Phases and Architectural Periodization of Vijayanagara Art
key_dimensions: Four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu — each with distinct but overlapping architectural contributions
Sangama phase: establishment of Hampi, early Virupaksha temple works, formative Dravidian style
Tuluva phase (especially Krishnadevaraya): peak of architectural achievement, elaboration of gopuram style
Aravidu phase and post-Battle of Talikota (1565): dispersal of art traditions to Deccan and southern regions

concepts.name: Stepped Temple Tanks (Pushkarini) and Water Architecture at Vijayanagara
key_dimensions: Architectural and engineering sophistication of stepped tanks (e.g., Pushkarini near Vitthala temple)
Integration of water bodies into the sacred landscape and ritual function (bathing before worship)
Vijayanagara hydraulic infrastructure: canals, sluices, and tanks as evidence of administrative and engineering capacity
Contrast between sacred pushkarinis (within temple complexes) and utilitarian irrigation tanks

concepts.name: Influence of Vijayanagara Art on Later South Indian Traditions
key_dimensions: Direct legacy in Nayaka architecture (Madurai, Thanjavur, Ikkeri Nayakas) — examinable continuity question
Elaboration of the Rayagopuram style into the massive gopurams of Madurai Meenakshi and Srirangam under Nayaka patronage
Transmission of the Vijayanagara painting style into Tanjore painting and Kerala mural traditions
Institutional continuity: devadasi system, temple management practices carried forward by successor states

concepts.name: Foreign Accounts as Sources for Vijayanagara Art and Architecture
key_dimensions: Key accounts: Abdur Razzaq (Persian, 1443), Nicolo Conti (Italian, ~1420), Domingo Paes (Portuguese, 1520s), Fernão Nunes (Portuguese, 1530s)
Descriptions of city splendor, bazaars, water channels, and royal festivals — corroborating archaeological evidence
UPSC trap: correctly attributing specific observations (e.g., Paes on Mahanavami festival vs. Razzaq on city layout)
Critical evaluation: foreign visitor biases, limited access to inner sanctums, and reliability as historical sources
